amendments.rule: A one-token source unit takes that token as its source head. In a multi-source unit choose the lexical or syntactic head. **Where one morpheme in the unit carries content the others do not, that morpheme is the head, whatever its position.** A construct noun fused with its preposition heads the unit — `לִפְנֵי` → *before*, `בְּתוֹךְ` → *among* — exactly as rule 30 directs; a negation heads the unit it is fused into, as rule 35 heads a `וְ` + `לֹא` *Nor* on the negative and rule 48 heads `מֵאֵין` → *without* on the `אַיִן`; and a relative heads a resumptive fusion, as rule 22 heads `אֲשֶׁר בּוֹ` → *wherein* on the relative. **Where no morpheme carries content the others lack — a compound preposition written from two prepositions, or a pair of particles — the syntactic head decides, and that is the morpheme governing the rest, which in Hebrew is the one standing first**: `מֵאֵת` → *of*, `מֵעַל` → *from* or *against*, `כַּאֲשֶׁר` → *as* and `הַאִם` → *shall* each head on their opening morpheme. **Two lexical morphemes may tie on exactly those terms, and what the morphemes are tagged is no part of the condition.** Where rule 30 fuses a construct chain, or a noun with its attributive, into a single English word that writes both lexemes — `עִקְּבֵי סוּס` → *horsehoofs*, `הֹלְכֵי נְתִיבוֹת` → *travellers*, `אֳרָחוֹת עֲקַלְקַלּוֹת` → *byways* — neither noun carries content the other lacks, since each one's sense stands inside the one English word, so the preceding sentence governs and the head is the morpheme governing the rest: the construct, or the noun the attributive modifies, which in Hebrew is the one standing first. This is rule 6's ruling that a rendering writing more than one morpheme's lexeme leaves none of them uniquely defensible, read for the source head of an `aligned` fusion rather than for the display anchor of a `noncompositional` one. But read whether both lexemes are written before reaching for it: where the single English word writes one noun's lexeme alone, this rule's first sentence governs and that morpheme heads, as `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* heads on `זוֹנָה` under rule 30. **The English word written is not what chooses a source head.** Rule 24's cross-language anchoring governs the target head alone, so do not move the source head onto the morpheme whose own sense the single English word happens to carry: one and the same `מֵעַל` rendered *from* in one verse and *against* in the next is one construction with one source head, and reading it off the translation would make the source analysis a function of the ASV's choice of preposition. Where two morphemes genuinely tie, choose and name the competing reading in the note under rule 8.
amendments.why: JDG.5.6 (twice) and JDG.5.22 fuse two full lexical nouns into one English word under rule 30's own sentence that 'a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme', and then have no rule telling them which morpheme is the source head: rule 23's first sentence does not decide, because each noun's sense stands inside the one English word, and its second sentence names only compound prepositions and pairs of particles, so a reader could take the tie-break as not reaching a lexical pair at all. The amendment widens that second sentence on its own stated ground — no morpheme carries content the others lack — rather than adding a cross-reference, and keeps rule 30's `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* untouched by requiring that both lexemes actually be written. Rule 6 already reasons this way for the display anchor of a fused phrase whose rendering writes several morphemes' lexemes, and nothing in the corpus tables supplied contradicts heading such a fusion on the governing morpheme.

conventions: Where a colon gaps its verb and the ASV writes that verb's English twice, both occurrences are the one written verb's discontinuous unit under rules 25 and 34, headed on the first English occurrence even where that occurrence is the ASV's supplied italic: JDG.5.14 gives the italic *came down* of the Ephraim colon and the written *came down* of the Machir colon to the one יָרְדוּ, headed on the italic, and JDG.5.28 gives *cried* and the italic second *cried* to the one תְּיַבֵּב, headed on the plain first. The italic corroborates and decides nothing (rule 7), and being italic does not disqualify a token from being the display anchor.

report: Read all 52 candidate lemma groups end to end. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by the ASV's own choice of word or by a morpheme present in one context and absent in the other: עַם takes a supplied *the* in 5.2 where no article stands and only *people* in 5.9 where the assimilated [הַ] takes the written *the*; בְּ is unrepresented in 5.14 where the ASV promotes its object to the object of *handle* (rule 40) and written *in* in 5.25; אַדִּיר is substantival in 5.13 (*the nobles*) and attributive in 5.25 (*lordly*, rule 28); מִפְּנֵי splits in 5.5 because the ASV writes both *at* and *presence*, while בְּעֵבֶר fuses in 5.17. That is rule 30's condition working, not two analyses.

The candidate table is blind to added units, so the chapter's eleven were checked against the dump directly. Supplied determiners (5.4, 5.7, 5.10, 5.13, 5.15, 5.19, 5.21, 5.22, 5.30), vocative *O*/*ye*/*thou* (5.3, 5.10, 5.12, 5.21, 5.31), the relative of a substantival participle (5.10, 5.14, 5.23, 5.31), and every construction-supplied copula or presentative frame (5.8, 5.14, 5.15, 5.16, 5.18, 5.31) are folded into the morpheme that licenses them in every verse; every coordinator no waw answers to (*and* 5.13, 5.19, 5.25; *even* 5.3, 5.5, 5.11), every supplied object pronoun (5.25 twice, 5.29), and the clause relative of 5.18 are added in every verse. No verse folds one of these in where another marks it out.

The one apparent tension is JDG.5.26, where *with the hammer* joins הָלְמָה while the supplied *him* of 5.25 is added. That is rule 44's own lexeme test rather than two conventions: *hammer* writes הָלַם's lexeme and *him* writes nothing. A third reading is available there that the verse note does not name — הַלְמוּת stands written in the preceding colon, so rule 25's resumed-referent amendment could give the second *the hammer* to that noun's discontinuous unit. Left as the verse pass decided, since the pass's reading is squarely rule 44's and re-cutting it on a tie is not what this pass is for; recorded here so a later reader can act on it.

Doubled English realizations of a once-written verb are handled alike in 5.14 (italic *came down* beside the written יָרְדוּ) and 5.28 (italic second *cried*), both under rules 25 and 34 and both headed on the first English occurrence. That the first occurrence in 5.14 is itself the ASV's italic supply is the only judgment a later reader would have to rediscover, so it is recorded in the log.

BSB disagreements: all five are documented convention differences, none an error. JDG.5.1.011 is the agreement article of בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, which rule 41 leaves unrepresented beside the single written *that* the demonstrative takes; JDG.5.1.013 is the לְ of לֵאמֹר (rule 27); JDG.5.14.021 is the בְּ whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object (rule 40); JDG.5.15.003 and JDG.5.29.009 are suffixes for which the ASV writes no possessive at all (*the princes of Issachar*, *returned answer*), the first with a margin the printed text overrides (rule 38). No accepted edge was moved for the aggregate.

One head worth naming though not a split: 5.11 reads *Far from* as one rendering of מִן headed on *from*, on the model of rule 24's *more than*; the competing reading leaves *Far* added, and the verse note carries it.
